learn.hook: A student who interviews 50 chaiwalas about their earnings has primary data. The student who later reads her report has secondary data. Same numbers, different labels!
points: Data are the values of variables; each recorded value is an observation. Data help explain economic problems such as low farm income.
Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for the purpose of the enquiry, e.g. through a survey or interview.
Secondary data have already been collected and processed by another agency, e.g. Census reports or RBI publications. They save time and money.
The same data are primary for the agency that collected them and secondary for anyone who uses them later.
Choice depends on purpose, time and money: primary data are original and suited to the purpose but costly; secondary data are cheap but must be checked for suitability and reliability.

example.q: A student wants to know the average pocket money in her school. She (a) surveys 60 classmates herself, and (b) also reads a newspaper report on teenagers' spending. Classify each source.
steps: (a) She collects the data first-hand for her enquiry: primary data.
(b) The newspaper collected and published the figures earlier: secondary data for her.

learn.reallife: NSO publishes the Periodic Labour Force Survey. For NSO it is primary data; for a journalist writing about jobs from that report it is secondary data.

games.title: Primary or secondary (for the person using it)?
items: A researcher personally interviewing 100 farmers
A student using Census 2011 tables
A company surveying its own customers by phone
An economist quoting figures from the Economic Survey
A teacher recording the heights of her students
A report using RBI's published inflation numbers
An NGO counting street children in a ward itself

games.title: Data facts
items: Secondary data are always more accurate than primary data.
Secondary data may have been collected for another purpose and must be checked.
The same data can be primary for one user and secondary for another.
It depends on who collected them.
Primary data usually cost more time and money to collect.
The investigator must plan and run the survey.
Each value of a variable that is recorded is called an observation.
Data are a collection of observations.
Secondary data are collected by the investigator for the first time.
That describes primary data.

quiz.q: Data collected by the investigator himself for the first time for a specific purpose are called:
quiz.explain: First-hand data collected for the enquiry are primary data.
steps: Asked: the name for data collected first-hand by the investigator for a specific purpose.
Rule: first-hand data collected for the enquiry itself are primary data.
Secondary data are collected by someone else; 'published' and 'grouped' describe form, not source.
So the answer is 'Primary data'.
Answer: Primary data
quiz.mistake: Mixes up primary and secondary

quiz.q: Which is an example of secondary data for a student project?
options: Counting vehicles at a crossing herself
Tables from the NSS report on household consumption
quiz.explain: The NSS report was collected by another agency, so it is secondary data for her.
steps: Asked: which source is secondary data for the student.
Rule: data already collected by another agency are secondary for the new user.
Interviewing, counting vehicles and asking heights are all done by her → primary.
NSS report tables were collected by another agency → secondary.
Answer: Tables from the NSS report on household consumption
quiz.mistake: Thinks any official-looking data is primary

quiz.q: Census 2011 data are primary for:
options: The office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, which collected them
quiz.explain: Data are primary for the agency that collected them first-hand.
steps: Asked: for whom Census 2011 data are primary.
Rule: data are primary for the agency that collected them first-hand.
The Census office (Registrar General and Census Commissioner) collected them.
For students, newspapers and other researchers the same data are secondary.
Answer: The office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, which collected them
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 'primary' depends on who collected the data

quiz.q: A main advantage of secondary data is that they:
options: Are always tailor-made for your purpose
quiz.explain: Someone else has already collected them, so you save time and money.
steps: Asked: the main advantage of secondary data.
Someone else has already collected the data.
So the user saves time and cost.
They may not fit your purpose and can contain errors → 'Save time and cost'.
Answer: Save time and cost
quiz.mistake: Assumes secondary data are always suitable and error-free

quiz.q: A researcher has very little time and money but needs state-wise literacy rates. The most sensible choice is:
options: Use published secondary data such as Census tables
quiz.explain: With limited time and money, reliable published data are the practical choice.
steps: Asked: the sensible choice with little time and money for state-wise literacy rates.
A fresh census is far too costly; guessing or one interview per state is unreliable.
Reliable published data already exist in Census tables.
So use published secondary data such as Census tables.
Answer: Use published secondary data such as Census tables
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary data are always better regardless of cost

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Before using secondary data, the investigator should check their reliability and suitability.
Reason (R): Secondary data were collected by someone else, possibly for a different purpose.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because they were gathered for another purpose, they may not fit or be reliable, so checking is needed.
steps: A: check reliability and suitability before using secondary data → true.
R: secondary data were collected by someone else, maybe for another purpose → true.
Because they were collected for another purpose, they may not fit or be reliable.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Trusts secondary data blindly

quiz.q: A survey records the monthly incomes of 25 households. How many observations of the variable 'income' does it have?
quiz.explain: Each household's recorded income is one observation, so there are 25.
steps: Given: monthly incomes of 25 households are recorded.
Rule: each recorded value of a variable is one observation.
One income per household → 25 × 1 = 25 observations.
So the answer is 25.
Answer: 25
quiz.mistake: Thinks the whole data set is a single observation

quiz.q: Which of these describes data as used in statistics?
options: Values of variables, each recorded value being an observation
quiz.explain: Data are recorded values of variables; each value is an observation.
steps: Asked: what data mean in statistics.
Rule: data are recorded values of variables.
Each recorded value is called an observation.
Data are not only opinions, newspaper numbers or descriptions → 'Values of variables, each recorded value being an observation'.
Answer: Values of variables, each recorded value being an observation
quiz.mistake: Thinks data must be published to count as data

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I read Census figures in a newspaper. Did I collect primary data? Teach me the difference!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Primary = I collect first-hand; secondary = already collected by someone else, cheaper and quicker!
teach.nudge: Hmm, who collected the Census data first? And what is the benefit of using data someone else collected?

revise.summary: Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for the enquiry; secondary data have already been collected and processed by another agency. The same data are primary for the collector and secondary for later users.
focus: Classify a data source as primary or secondary
Explain why 'primary' depends on who collected the data
Compare primary and secondary data on suitability, cost and time
Know that each recorded value of a variable is an observation
remember: Primary data: collected first-hand by the investigator for the purpose of the enquiry
Secondary data: already collected and processed by another agency, e.g. Census reports or RBI publications
traps: Don't think official-looking data are always primary: they are secondary for anyone who did not collect them
Don't trust secondary data blindly: check their suitability and reliability
Don't assume primary data are always better regardless of time and cost

learn.hook: 'Don't you think our tasty noodles are better than other brands?' That one question breaks at least two rules of survey design. Let's learn to spot them.
points: A survey collects information from individuals using an instrument: a questionnaire (filled by the respondent) or an interview schedule (filled by the interviewer).
A good questionnaire is short, clear and precise, and moves logically from general to specific questions.
Avoid: ambiguous words ('often', 'regularly'), double negatives ('Don't you not…'), leading questions that hint at an answer, and questions that need calculations.
Closed-ended questions give fixed choices: two-way (yes/no) or multiple-choice. They are easy to tabulate but harder to frame well.
Open-ended questions allow free answers ('What do you think of…?'). They give rich detail but are hard to compare and interpret.

example.q: Improve this question: 'You don't think smoking is not harmful, do you?'
steps: Problem 1: double negative ('don't… not') confuses the respondent.
Problem 2: it leads the respondent towards an answer.
Rewrite as a neutral closed question: 'In your opinion, is smoking harmful to health?' (Yes / No / Can't say).
example.answer: 'In your opinion, is smoking harmful to health? Yes / No / Can't say'

learn.reallife: Before every big election, survey agencies frame neutral, short questions so that responses from lakhs of voters can be compared quickly.

games.title: Good or bad question?
items: What is your age in completed years?
Don't you think this soap is the best?
Do you own a two-wheeler? Yes / No
How much did your family spend on food per day last year, multiplied by 365?
Do you watch TV often?
Which brand of noodles do you buy most? A / B / C / Other
Are you not unhappy with the bus service?

games.title: Match the flaw to the question
pairs: 'Wouldn't you agree prices are too high?'
'What is your yearly income if your monthly income is ₹18,500?'
'Do you own a bicycle? Yes / No'

quiz.q: Which of the following is a two-way question?
options: Do you have a bank account? Yes / No
What is your opinion of online classes?
Which of these four brands do you prefer?
How can the bus service be improved?
quiz.explain: A two-way question offers exactly two possible answers, such as yes or no.
steps: Asked: which is a two-way question.
Rule: a two-way question allows exactly two answers, such as Yes / No.
'Do you have a bank account? Yes / No' has just two choices.
The others are open-ended or have four choices → the bank account question.
Answer: Do you have a bank account? Yes / No
quiz.mistake: Confuses two-way with multiple-choice

quiz.q: 'Don't you agree that our new phone is the best in the market?' is a poor question mainly because it is:
quiz.explain: It pushes the respondent towards agreeing.
steps: Asked: what is wrong with 'Don't you agree that our new phone is the best?'.
Rule: a leading question pushes the respondent towards a particular answer.
The wording invites the person to agree.
So it is a poor question mainly because it is leading.
Answer: Leading
quiz.mistake: Notices the question but not the hint built into it

quiz.q: A questionnaire should generally move from:
quiz.explain: Starting with general questions eases the respondent into the specific ones.
steps: Asked: the order in which questions should move.
Rule: start with general questions, then go to specific ones.
General questions ease the respondent into the survey.
So the correct order is general to specific.
Answer: General to specific questions
quiz.mistake: Reverses the logical order

quiz.q: The main disadvantage of open-ended questions is that the answers are:
quiz.explain: Free answers vary widely in content and wording, so they are hard to tabulate and compare.
steps: Asked: the main drawback of open-ended questions.
Open-ended questions let people answer freely in their own words.
Such answers vary widely, so they are hard to tabulate, compare and interpret.
'Restricted to yes or no' describes two-way questions → 'Difficult to compare and interpret'.
Answer: Difficult to compare and interpret
quiz.mistake: Confuses open-ended with closed-ended questions

quiz.q: Which question avoids ambiguity best?
options: How many hours did you study yesterday?
Do you often go to the library?
quiz.explain: It asks for a precise, measurable answer about a fixed time.
steps: Asked: the question that best avoids ambiguity.
Words like 'a lot', 'good' and 'often' mean different things to different people.
'How many hours did you study yesterday?' asks for a precise number for a fixed day.
So that question avoids ambiguity best.
Answer: How many hours did you study yesterday?
quiz.mistake: Accepts vague words like 'a lot' or 'often'

quiz.q: Which question should NOT be put in a questionnaire?
options: What is your monthly household income? (choose a range)
Do you use a smartphone? Yes / No
If you spend ₹45 a day on travel, what do you spend in a leap year?
quiz.explain: Questions that require calculation burden the respondent and cause errors.
steps: Asked: the question that should NOT be in a questionnaire.
Rule: avoid questions that make the respondent calculate.
Working out ₹45 × days of a leap year burdens the respondent and causes errors.
The income range, smartphone and newspaper questions are fine → the leap-year question.
Answer: If you spend ₹45 a day on travel, what do you spend in a leap year?
quiz.mistake: Does not see calculation questions as a fault

quiz.q: A firm surveying the popularity of its noodles wants answers it can tabulate easily. It should mostly use:
quiz.explain: Closed-ended questions give fixed options that are quick to count and compare.
steps: Asked: the question type that gives easily tabulated answers.
Closed-ended (multiple-choice) questions give fixed options.
Fixed options are quick to count and compare.
Open-ended, leading and double-negative questions do not help → closed-ended questions.
Answer: Closed-ended (multiple-choice) questions
quiz.mistake: Thinks open-ended questions are easier to tabulate

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Closed-ended questions are easy to analyse.
Reason (R): Closed-ended questions are always easy to frame.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Closed questions are easy to analyse, but framing complete and unbiased options is actually difficult.
steps: A: closed-ended questions are easy to analyse → true.
R: closed-ended questions are always easy to frame → false.
Framing complete and unbiased options is actually difficult.
So A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Assumes ease of analysis means ease of framing

teach.ask: Gappu wants to survey his flock: 'Isn't my song the best, don't you think?' Teach me how to write good survey questions.
teach.praise: Tweet! Short, clear, no leading hints, no double negatives, and choose closed or open questions wisely!
teach.nudge: Good! But my question hints at the answer. What is that flaw called, and what other traps should I avoid?

revise.summary: A survey uses a questionnaire or an interview schedule. A good questionnaire is short, clear and precise, moves from general to specific, and avoids ambiguous, double-negative, leading and calculation questions.
focus: Spot and fix faulty questions: ambiguous, double negative, leading, needing calculation
Tell two-way and multiple-choice (closed-ended) questions from open-ended ones
Compare closed-ended and open-ended questions: ease of tabulation vs rich detail
Know the correct order: general to specific
remember: Questionnaire: filled by the respondent; interview schedule: filled by the interviewer
Closed-ended: two-way (yes/no) or multiple-choice; open-ended: free answers
traps: Don't confuse two-way questions with multiple-choice questions
Easy to analyse does not mean easy to frame: closed-ended questions are harder to frame well
Don't accept vague words like 'often' or 'regularly' in a question

topics.title: Modes of data collection and the pilot survey

learn.hook: Want to survey tribal households in remote Bastar, college students in Pune, and shoppers at a Delhi mall? One method will not fit all three.
points: Personal interview: face-to-face questioning. Highest response, allows clarification and observation, but costly, slow, needs trained interviewers, and the interviewer may influence answers.

Mailing questionnaire (post, email, online form, SMS): cheapest, covers wide and remote areas, respondents answer privately, but response is low, no one can clarify doubts, and it needs literate respondents.
Telephone interview: cheaper and quicker than personal visits, allows some clarification, but reaches only people with phones and loses face-to-face cues like body language.
Pilot survey: a small trial survey before the main one. It tests the questionnaire's clarity, the instructions, the enumerators' performance, and estimates cost and time.

example.q: Choose a mode: a researcher must survey 5,000 graduates across India within a week and with a small budget.
steps: Personal interviews across India in a week: too slow and costly.
Telephone: possible but costly for 5,000 people in a week.
Online/mailed questionnaire: cheap, fast and graduates are literate and connected.
example.answer: An online (mailed) questionnaire, perhaps with phone follow-ups for non-response.

learn.reallife: Before Census operations, enumerators run a pre-test (a pilot) in selected areas to see which questions confuse people, and the forms are revised.

games.title: Match the mode to its feature
pairs: Interviewer can observe and clarify, but costly
Cheapest and wide coverage, but low response
Quick, but only reaches people with phones
Small trial to test the questionnaire

games.title: Which mode suits best?
items: Survey of non-literate farm workers in a village
Survey of 10,000 software engineers across cities
Quick follow-up with 200 known customers who own phones
Detailed study needing observation of living conditions
Low-budget survey of literate people in remote areas
Calling 300 shopkeepers who have phones but no internet for a same-day opinion poll

quiz.q: Which method of data collection gives the highest response rate?
quiz.explain: Face-to-face contact makes refusals less likely and lets the interviewer clarify questions.
steps: Asked: the method with the highest response rate.
In a personal interview the investigator meets the respondent face to face.
Refusals are less likely and doubts can be cleared on the spot.
Mailed, online and phone methods get fewer replies → 'Personal interview'.
Answer: Personal interview
quiz.mistake: Thinks cheaper methods give better response

quiz.q: A major disadvantage of the mailing questionnaire method is:
quiz.explain: Many people do not return mailed or emailed questionnaires.
steps: Asked: a major disadvantage of the mailing questionnaire.
Many people simply do not return mailed or emailed questionnaires.
Mailing is cheap and covers a wide area, and there is no interviewer bias.
So the disadvantage is 'Low response rate'.
Answer: Low response rate
quiz.mistake: Confuses the disadvantages of different modes

quiz.q: The telephone interview method cannot be used for people who:
options: Do not have access to a phone
quiz.explain: Only people with phones can be reached.
steps: Asked: who cannot be reached by a telephone interview.
A telephone interview needs the respondent to have a phone.
People without access to a phone are left out.
Literacy, city living or a job do not stop a phone call → 'Do not have access to a phone'.
Answer: Do not have access to a phone
quiz.mistake: Ignores the access limitation of phone surveys

quiz.q: Which mode is most suitable for a survey of non-literate respondents?
quiz.explain: An interviewer can read the questions aloud and record answers.
steps: Asked: the best mode for non-literate respondents.
Mailed, online and SMS surveys need the respondent to read and write.
In a personal interview the interviewer reads questions aloud and records the answers.
So the answer is 'Personal interview'.
Answer: Personal interview
quiz.mistake: Forgets that mailed questionnaires need literate respondents

quiz.q: A pilot survey is conducted:
options: Before the main survey as a small trial
After the main survey to check results
quiz.explain: It is a trial run to test the questionnaire and estimate cost and time.
steps: Asked: when a pilot survey is conducted.
Rule: a pilot survey is a small trial run before the main survey.
It tests the questionnaire and estimates cost and time.
It comes before, not after, and does not replace the main survey.
Answer: Before the main survey as a small trial
quiz.mistake: Thinks a pilot survey is done after the main survey

quiz.q: Which is NOT a purpose of a pilot survey?
options: Estimating the cost and time of the main survey
Replacing the need for a main survey
quiz.explain: A pilot survey prepares for the main survey; it does not replace it.
steps: Asked: which is NOT a purpose of a pilot survey.
A pilot survey tests questions, estimates cost and time, and checks enumerators.
It only prepares for the main survey.
So 'Replacing the need for a main survey' is not a purpose.
Answer: Replacing the need for a main survey
quiz.mistake: Thinks the trial results are enough

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a personal interview, the respondent's answers may be influenced by the interviewer.
Reason (R): The interviewer is physically present and may unintentionally suggest answers.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The interviewer's presence, tone or expressions can bias answers.
steps: A: answers in a personal interview may be influenced by the interviewer → true.
R: the interviewer is present and may unintentionally suggest answers → true.
The interviewer's presence, tone or expressions can bias answers, which is why A happens.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Assumes personal interviews have no drawbacks

quiz.q: A survey team mails 800 questionnaires and gets 200 back. What is the response rate?
quiz.explain: Response rate = 200/800 × 100 = 25%. Low response is typical of mailed surveys.
steps: Response rate = returned / sent × 100
Answer: 25%
quiz.mistake: Divides 800 by 200 or reports the non-response

teach.ask: Gappu must survey birds all over the forest with very little money. 'Which method should I choose? Teach me the modes!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Personal, mailed or phone, each with pros and cons, and a pilot survey first to test my questions!
teach.nudge: Good! You named some methods. What about a small test run before the real survey?

revise.summary: Data can be collected by personal interview, mailing questionnaire or telephone interview, each with its own merits and drawbacks. A pilot survey is a small trial run before the main survey.
focus: Compare the three modes on response, cost, clarification and reach
Choose a suitable mode for a given situation (budget, time, literacy)
State the purposes of a pilot survey
Calculate a response rate
remember: Personal interview: highest response but costly and slow; mailing: cheapest but low response and needs literate respondents
Pilot survey: a small trial before the main survey to test the questionnaire, instructions and enumerators, and estimate cost and time
traps: Don't think cheaper methods give better response
A pilot survey is done before the main survey, not after it, and it does not replace it
Don't forget phone surveys reach only people who have phones

learn.hook: To know if the dal is cooked, you taste one spoonful, not the whole pot. That spoonful is a sample.
points: Population (universe): all the items or units under study, e.g. all farms in a district.
Census (complete enumeration): data collected from every unit of the population. The Census of India is held every 10 years and counts every person.
Sample: a group of units drawn from the population that represents it. A good sample is representative.
Advantages of a sample survey: cheaper, quicker, needs fewer staff, allows more detailed questions, and can give reasonably accurate results.
A census is preferred when every unit matters (e.g. population count, voter lists) or when the population is small; a sample is needed when testing destroys items (e.g. testing bulbs).

example.q: A researcher studies 50 out of 200 farms in a village to estimate average yield of wheat per acre. Identify the population, sample and variable.
steps: Population = all units under study = 200 farms.
Sample = units actually surveyed = 50 farms.
Variable = the characteristic measured = wheat yield per acre.
example.answer: Population: 200 farms; sample: 50 farms; variable: yield per acre.

learn.reallife: India's population grew from about 23.8 crore in 1901 to about 121 crore in 2011, a fact known only because the Census counted everyone.

games.title: Census or sample?
items: Counting every person in India
Testing the life of electric bulbs from a factory
Preparing the voter list of a constituency
Checking the quality of rice in a godown
Estimating the average TV viewing time of Indians
Recording marks of all 40 students in a class

games.title: Census vs sample
items: A sample survey is generally cheaper than a census.
Fewer units are studied.
A census covers every unit of the population.
That is complete enumeration.
A sample can never give accurate results.
A well-chosen, representative sample gives reasonably accurate results.
When testing destroys the item, a sample must be used.
Testing every item would destroy the whole stock.
The Census of India is held every 5 years.
It is held every 10 years.
Population means only people in statistics.
Population is all units under study, e.g. farms, firms or bulbs.

quiz.q: In statistics, 'population' means:
options: Only the people living in a country
A part of the units under study
Only the units with data errors
quiz.explain: Population (universe) is the complete set of items being studied.
steps: Asked: the meaning of 'population' in statistics.
Rule: population (universe) = all the units under study.
It need not be people; it can be any items being studied.
'A part of the units' is a sample → 'All the units under study'.
Answer: All the units under study
quiz.mistake: Uses the everyday meaning of population

quiz.q: Complete enumeration of every unit of the population is called:
quiz.explain: A census covers every unit.
steps: Asked: the name for enumerating every unit of the population.
Rule: a census covers every single unit.
Sampling and a pilot survey cover only some units.
So the answer is 'Census'.
Answer: Census
quiz.mistake: Confuses census with sampling

quiz.q: A study selects 300 households out of 6,000 households in a town. What percentage of the population is in the sample?
steps: Sample share = 300 / 6,000 × 100
Answer: 5%
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way or slips a decimal

quiz.q: In a study of the monthly expenditure of 80 students chosen from a college of 1,600, the variable is:
quiz.explain: The variable is the characteristic being measured: monthly expenditure.
steps: Asked: the variable in a study of monthly expenditure of 80 students from 1,600.
Rule: the variable is the characteristic being measured.
1,600 students = population, 80 students = sample.
The thing measured is 'Monthly expenditure'.
Answer: Monthly expenditure
quiz.mistake: Confuses the variable with the population or sample

quiz.q: Which situation requires a sample rather than a census?
options: Counting all voters for an electoral roll
Counting students present in class today
Listing all bank branches in a city
quiz.explain: Testing destroys matchsticks, so only a sample can be tested.
steps: Asked: a situation that needs a sample rather than a census.
Testing a matchstick by striking it destroys it.
If every matchstick were tested, none would be left to sell.
Voters, students present and bank branches can all be counted fully → the matchstick test.
Answer: Testing matchsticks by striking them
quiz.mistake: Does not see destructive testing as a reason to sample

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A sample survey can collect more detailed information than a census with the same budget.
Reason (R): A sample covers fewer units, so more time and money can be spent on each unit.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With fewer units, resources can go into detailed, careful questioning.
steps: A: a sample can collect more detail than a census on the same budget → true.
R: a sample has fewer units, so more time and money can go to each unit → true.
Spending more on each unit is exactly why the sample gets more detail.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks a census always gives more detail

quiz.q: A good sample should be:
quiz.explain: It must reflect the features of the population to give reliable estimates.
steps: Asked: the key quality of a good sample.
A sample is used to estimate the features of the population.
So it must reflect the population, i.e. be representative.
Friends or very small samples give biased results → 'Representative of the population'.
Answer: Representative of the population
quiz.mistake: Thinks convenience is enough for a sample

quiz.q: India's population was about 23.8 crore in 1901 and about 121 crore in 2011. Roughly how many times did it grow?
quiz.explain: 121 ÷ 23.8 ≈ 5.1, so about five times in 110 years.
steps: Growth factor = 121 / 23.8
Answer: About 5 times
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of dividing, or misreads the units

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know how sweet all the mangoes on a tree are. 'Must I eat every mango? Teach me census and sample!'
teach.praise: Tweet! A census checks every mango; a representative sample checks a few, cheaper and quicker!
teach.nudge: Good! But what makes a sample trustworthy? And why not just check every mango?

revise.summary: A census collects data from every unit of the population, while a sample survey studies a representative group drawn from it. Samples are cheaper and quicker; a census is preferred when every unit matters.
focus: Identify the population, sample and variable in a study
List the advantages of a sample survey
Decide when a census or a sample is needed (e.g. destructive testing)
Find what percentage of the population is in the sample
remember: Population (universe): all the items or units under study
Census (complete enumeration): data from every unit; the Census of India is held every 10 years
traps: 'Population' in statistics means all units under study, not just people
Don't confuse the variable with the population or the sample
A good sample must be representative, not just convenient

learn.hook: Exit polls on election day interview a few thousand voters and try to predict the votes of crores. Sometimes they nail it; sometimes they miss badly. Sampling method makes the difference.
points: Random sampling: every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected. The investigator has no say in who is chosen.
Lottery method: write each unit's name on a slip, mix well, draw the required number. Random number tables or computer-generated random numbers do the same for large populations.
Sampling frame: the complete list of units of the population from which the sample is drawn (e.g. a voters' list).

Non-random sampling: units do not have an equal chance of selection. Types: judgement/purposive (investigator's choice), convenience (easy to reach) and quota (fixed numbers from each group). Bias is likely.
The number of ways of choosing r units from N is ᴺCᵣ = N! / (r!(N − r)!), e.g. 3 students out of 10 can be chosen in 120 ways.

example.q: How many different samples of 3 students can be drawn from a class of 10?

learn.reallife: Exit polls sample voters at chosen booths. If the booths or voters chosen are not representative, or people do not answer honestly, the prediction can go wrong.

games.title: Random or non-random?
items: Drawing names from a box after mixing slips
Interviewing whoever is standing near the college gate
Using a computer to pick 50 roll numbers at random
Choosing the 'most typical' villages by the researcher's judgement
Selecting exactly 20 men and 20 women as they come
Using random number tables to pick households

games.title: Match the method to its description
pairs: Units easiest to reach are chosen
Investigator picks units he thinks typical
Fixed number of units from each group

quiz.q: In random sampling:
options: Every unit has an equal chance of being selected
The investigator chooses the units he likes
Only the largest units are selected
quiz.explain: Equal chance of selection is the defining feature of random sampling.
steps: Asked: the feature of random sampling.
Rule: in random sampling every unit has an equal chance of being selected.
The investigator's liking or convenience plays no part.
So the answer is 'Every unit has an equal chance of being selected'.
Answer: Every unit has an equal chance of being selected
quiz.mistake: Confuses random with haphazard or convenient selection

quiz.q: How many different samples of 2 can be drawn from 6 households?
steps: Answer: 15
quiz.mistake: Uses 6 × 5 = 30 and forgets that order does not matter

quiz.q: How many different samples of 3 students can be chosen from 10 students?
steps: Answer: 120
quiz.mistake: Stops at 10 × 9 × 8 = 720 and forgets to divide by 3!

quiz.q: The list of all units of the population from which a sample is drawn is called the:
quiz.explain: A sampling frame is the full list, like a voters' list or school register.
steps: Asked: the name for the full list of units from which a sample is drawn.
Rule: this list is the sampling frame, e.g. a voters' list or school register.
A questionnaire is a set of questions, not a list of units.
So the answer is 'Sampling frame'.
Answer: Sampling frame
quiz.mistake: Confuses the list of units with the survey instrument

quiz.q: Choosing respondents simply because they are easy to reach is:
quiz.explain: Convenience sampling picks easily accessible units, so bias is likely.
steps: Asked: the name for choosing respondents because they are easy to reach.
Rule: picking easily accessible units is convenience sampling.
It is non-random, so bias is likely.
Lottery and random sampling give equal chances → 'Convenience sampling'.
Answer: Convenience sampling
quiz.mistake: Thinks any unplanned selection is random

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Non-random sampling may give biased results.
Reason (R): In non-random sampling, all units do not have an equal chance of being selected.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Unequal chances let the investigator's choice or convenience distort the sample.
steps: A: non-random sampling may give biased results → true.
R: in non-random sampling all units do not have an equal chance → true.
Unequal chances let choice or convenience distort the sample, causing bias.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between unequal chance and bias

quiz.q: A lottery is drawn, but the slips for some names are folded differently and are easier to pick. Is the sample still random?
options: Yes, because a lottery always gives a random sample
Yes, if the box is large
No, because the units no longer have an equal chance of selection
No, because lotteries are never random
quiz.explain: A lottery is random only if every slip is identical and well mixed, giving each unit an equal chance.
steps: Rule: a lottery is random only if all slips are identical and well mixed.
Here some slips are folded differently and are easier to pick.
So some units have a better chance than others.
The sample is not random → 'No, because the units no longer have an equal chance of selection'.
Answer: No, because the units no longer have an equal chance of selection
quiz.mistake: Believes the lottery method guarantees randomness automatically

quiz.q: Why can an exit poll go wrong?
options: The sample of voters may not represent all voters, or voters may not answer honestly
quiz.explain: Unrepresentative booths or untruthful answers bias the estimate.
steps: Asked: why an exit poll can go wrong.
An exit poll asks only a sample of voters.
If the chosen voters do not represent all voters, or do not answer honestly, the estimate is biased.
Exit polls do not interview every voter → 'The sample of voters may not represent all voters, or voters may not answer honestly'.
Answer: The sample of voters may not represent all voters, or voters may not answer honestly
quiz.mistake: Thinks a sample-based prediction must always be right or always wrong

teach.ask: Gappu must pick 5 birds out of 30 for a choir test. 'How do I pick fairly? Teach me random sampling!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Give every bird an equal chance, using a lottery or random numbers, and avoid biased judgement picks!
teach.nudge: Nice! But how exactly would you make sure each bird has the same chance? Name a method.

revise.summary: In random sampling every unit has an equal chance of selection, as in the lottery method or random number tables. In non-random sampling (judgement, convenience, quota) units do not have an equal chance, so bias is likely.
focus: Define random sampling and the lottery method
Name the types of non-random sampling
Count possible samples using ᴺCᵣ
Explain why an exit poll can go wrong
remember: Random sampling: every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected
Sampling frame: the complete list of units from which the sample is drawn
ᴺCᵣ = N! / (r!(N − r)!); 3 students out of 10 can be chosen in 120 ways
traps: Random does not mean haphazard or convenient selection
Don't stop at 10 × 9 × 8: divide by r! because order does not matter
A lottery is random only if every slip is identical and well mixed

learn.hook: Your sample says farmers in a village earn ₹600 a day on average. The truth is ₹580. That ₹20 gap has a name, and so do the much nastier errors that no sample size can fix.
points: Sampling error = sample estimate − true population value (the gap is often stated as a size). It arises because only part of the population is observed.
Sampling error falls as the sample size rises; it disappears in a census.
Non-sampling errors can occur in both a census and a sample survey, are more serious, and are harder to detect and control.

Types: sampling bias (the sampling method excludes some units, e.g. a phone survey missing people without phones); non-response (people do not reply); errors in data acquisition (wrong recording, measurement mistakes, misunderstood questions, false answers).
Non-sampling errors can be reduced by careful questionnaire design, training enumerators and follow-ups, but not by simply enlarging the sample.

example.q: Five farmers earn ₹500, ₹550, ₹600, ₹650 and ₹700 a day. A sample of two picks ₹600 and ₹700. Find the sampling error.
steps: Sampling error = 650 − 600 = ₹50.

learn.reallife: Surveys on household spending face non-response when wealthy households refuse to take part, which can understate average consumption, an error a bigger sample alone cannot fix.

games.title: Sampling or non-sampling error?
items: Sample mean differs from population mean by chance
Enumerator writes 45 instead of 54
Many households refuse to answer
A phone survey misses people without phones
Estimate changes when a different random sample is drawn
Respondent misunderstands a question

games.title: Errors true or false
items: Sampling error can be reduced by increasing sample size.
Larger samples give estimates closer to the true value.
Non-sampling errors occur only in sample surveys.
They occur in census too, e.g. recording mistakes.
A census has no sampling error.
Every unit is covered, so there is no sample-population gap.
Non-sampling errors are usually easier to control than sampling errors.
They are harder to detect and control.
Non-response is a type of non-sampling error.
Missing replies can bias results.

quiz.q: Sampling error is the difference between:
options: The sample estimate and the actual population value
quiz.explain: It is the gap between what the sample says and the true population value.
steps: Asked: the meaning of sampling error.
Rule: sampling error = sample estimate − actual population value.
It arises because only a part of the population is studied.
So it is the difference between the sample estimate and the actual population value.
Answer: The sample estimate and the actual population value
quiz.mistake: Thinks sampling error means a mistake by the enumerator

quiz.q: Population of 5 incomes: ₹200, ₹300, ₹400, ₹500, ₹600. A sample picks ₹200 and ₹300. By how much does the sample mean underestimate the population mean?
quiz.explain: Population mean = 2,000/5 = ₹400. Sample mean = ₹250. The sample falls short by 400 − 250 = ₹150; this gap is the sampling error.
steps: Answer: ₹150
quiz.mistake: Reports the sample mean or the population mean instead of the gap

quiz.q: Population of 4 marks: 40, 50, 60, 70. A sample picks 60 and 70. What is the sampling error of the sample mean?
quiz.explain: Population mean = 55, sample mean = 65, so error = 65 − 55 = 10 (an overestimate).
steps: Population mean = 220/4 = 55
Sample mean = 130/2 = 65
Answer: 10
quiz.mistake: Reports the sample mean or flips the sign

quiz.q: Which of the following is a non-sampling error?
options: The sample mean differs from the population mean by chance
An enumerator records the wrong age
A larger sample gives a different estimate
Two random samples give slightly different means
quiz.explain: Recording mistakes are errors in data acquisition, a non-sampling error.
steps: Asked: which is a non-sampling error.
Chance differences between sample and population means are sampling errors.
An enumerator recording the wrong age is a mistake in collecting data.
Errors in data acquisition are non-sampling errors → the wrong-age option.
Answer: An enumerator records the wrong age
quiz.mistake: Confuses chance sampling variation with human errors

quiz.q: Sampling error can be reduced by:
options: Increasing the size of the sample
quiz.explain: Larger samples represent the population better.
steps: Asked: how to reduce sampling error.
A larger sample represents the population better.
So the gap between estimate and true value usually falls.
Leading questions or a smaller sample would make things worse → 'Increasing the size of the sample'.
Answer: Increasing the size of the sample
quiz.mistake: Thinks a smaller sample is more accurate

quiz.q: A telephone survey about internet use in a district misses all households without phones. This is:
quiz.explain: The method systematically excludes part of the population: sampling bias.
steps: Asked: the error when a phone survey misses all homes without phones.
The method itself leaves out a whole part of the population every time.
This systematic exclusion is sampling bias.
It is not due to chance or people refusing → 'Sampling bias'.
Answer: Sampling bias
quiz.mistake: Thinks any wrong estimate is just random sampling error

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Non-sampling errors can occur even in a census.
Reason (R): A census covers every unit of the population.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but covering every unit does not explain the errors; they come from recording, non-response and similar problems.
steps: A: non-sampling errors can occur even in a census → true.
R: a census covers every unit → true.
But covering every unit does not cause the errors; they come from recording mistakes, non-response, etc.
So both are true but R does not explain A.
Answer: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
quiz.mistake: Thinks complete coverage causes or removes non-sampling errors

quiz.q: Why are non-sampling errors considered more serious than sampling errors?
options: They occur only in small samples
They are harder to detect and do not fall just by increasing sample size
They can be calculated exactly by formula
quiz.explain: They arise from bias, non-response and recording errors, which a bigger sample does not remove.
steps: Asked: why non-sampling errors are more serious.
They come from bias, non-response and recording mistakes.
They are hard to detect and do not fall just by taking a bigger sample.
They are not 'always small' and cannot be calculated by formula → 'They are harder to detect and do not fall just by increasing sample size'.
Answer: They are harder to detect and do not fall just by increasing sample size
quiz.mistake: Thinks a larger sample fixes all errors

teach.ask: Gappu counted 10 nests and found the average eggs to be 4, but the forest's true average is 3. 'Did I make a mistake? Teach me about errors!'
teach.praise: Tweet! The gap between sample and truth is sampling error, which falls with a bigger sample; non-sampling errors are trickier!
teach.nudge: Good! Can a bigger sample cure every error? What about birds who refuse to answer or wrong records?

revise.summary: Sampling error is the gap between the sample estimate and the true population value; it falls as sample size rises and disappears in a census. Non-sampling errors (sampling bias, non-response, data acquisition errors) occur in both and are more serious.
focus: Calculate sampling error from a sample mean and the population mean
Classify an error as sampling or non-sampling, and name the type
Explain why non-sampling errors are more serious
Know how each kind of error can be reduced
remember: Sampling error = sample estimate − true population value
Non-sampling errors: sampling bias, non-response, errors in data acquisition
traps: Sampling error is not a mistake by the enumerator
Don't report the sample mean or population mean instead of the gap between them
A bigger sample does not fix non-sampling errors

topics.title: Census of India, NSSO and other data agencies

learn.hook: Every 10 years, lakhs of enumerators knock on every door in India, from Ladakh to Lakshadweep. It is one of the largest data operations on the planet.
points: Major national agencies: Census of India, National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), Central Statistical Office (CSO), Registrar General of India (RGI), Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCIS), and the Labour Bureau.

Census of India: the most complete source of demographic data (population size, density, sex ratio, literacy, migration). Held regularly every 10 years since 1881; the first Census after independence was in 1951.

NSSO (set up in 1950) runs nationwide sample surveys in 'rounds' on socio-economic issues such as consumer expenditure, employment, literacy and health. Results appear in reports and its journal 'Sarvekshana'. In 2019, NSSO and CSO were merged to form the National Statistical Office (NSO).
Other sources: CSO (national income), RGI (births and deaths), DGCIS (foreign trade), Labour Bureau (labour data); also the Economic Survey, RBI publications and international bodies.

example.q: A student needs data on (i) India's sex ratio, (ii) household consumption expenditure, (iii) India's exports. Which source fits each?
steps: (i) Sex ratio is demographic: Census of India.
(ii) Consumer expenditure surveys are run by NSSO (now NSO) in rounds.
(iii) Foreign trade statistics: DGCIS.

learn.reallife: Census 2011 was the 15th Census of India and the 7th after independence. Census data guide everything from seat allocation to planning schools and hospitals.

games.title: Match the agency to its data
pairs: Sample surveys on consumption and employment

items.text: The Census of India is conducted every ___ years.
The first Census after independence was held in ___.
The Census has been held regularly since ___.
NSSO publishes its survey findings in the journal ___.

quiz.q: The Census of India has been conducted regularly every ten years since:
quiz.explain: Regular decennial census began in 1881.
steps: Asked: the year from which India's Census has been held regularly every ten years.
Fact from the lesson: the regular decennial Census began in 1881.
The earlier attempt in 1872 was not part of the regular ten-year series.
So the answer is 1881.
Answer: 1881
quiz.mistake: Picks 1951, the first census after independence

quiz.q: The first Census of independent India was held in:
quiz.explain: It was conducted in 1951.
steps: Asked: the year of the first Census of independent India.
India became independent in 1947.
The first Census after independence was held in 1951 (ten years after 1941).
So the answer is 1951.
Answer: 1951
quiz.mistake: Assumes the census was held in the year of independence

quiz.q: Which agency conducts large-scale sample surveys in 'rounds' on consumer expenditure and employment?
quiz.explain: NSSO runs nationwide sample surveys in rounds.
steps: Asked: the agency that runs large sample surveys in 'rounds'.
Fact: NSSO conducts nationwide sample surveys in rounds on consumer expenditure and employment.
The Census is a complete count, not a sample survey; DGCIS compiles trade data.
So the answer is NSSO.
Answer: NSSO
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Census does these sample surveys

quiz.q: The journal in which NSSO publishes its survey results is:
quiz.explain: NSSO's journal is Sarvekshana.
steps: Asked: the journal in which NSSO publishes its survey results.
Fact from the lesson: NSSO's journal is 'Sarvekshana'.
Economic Survey is published by the Ministry of Finance.
So the answer is Sarvekshana.
Answer: Sarvekshana
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with other government publications

quiz.q: Data on India's foreign trade are compiled by:
quiz.explain: The Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics compiles trade data.
steps: Asked: the body that compiles India's foreign trade data.
Fact: the Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCIS) compiles trade data.
The Registrar General and Census handle population; NSSO runs sample surveys.
So the answer is DGCIS.
Answer: DGCIS
quiz.mistake: Links trade data to the Census

quiz.q: Census 2011 was the 7th Census after independence. If censuses are 10 years apart, in which year was the 1st post-independence census held?
quiz.explain: Counting back six gaps of 10 years from 2011 gives 2011 − 60 = 1951.
steps: 7 censuses means 6 gaps of 10 years
Answer: 1951
quiz.mistake: Counts seven gaps instead of six

quiz.q: Which of these is a secondary source of economic data published by the Ministry of Finance every year?
quiz.explain: The Economic Survey is released by the Ministry of Finance before the Union Budget.
steps: Asked: the yearly secondary source published by the Ministry of Finance.
Fact: the Economic Survey is released by the Ministry of Finance before the Union Budget.
Sarvekshana belongs to NSSO; Census tables come from the Census office.
So the answer is 'Economic Survey'.
Answer: Economic Survey
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Economic Survey with NSSO's journal

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The Census is the most complete source of demographic data in India.
Reason (R): The Census covers every household through complete enumeration.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because it enumerates everyone, it gives the fullest population data.
steps: A: the Census is the most complete source of demographic data in India → true.
R: the Census covers every household by complete enumeration → true.
Because it counts everyone, it gives the fullest population data.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect complete coverage with completeness of data

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Who counts all the people in India, and who asks families how much they spend? Teach me the data agencies!'
teach.praise: Tweet! The Census counts everyone every 10 years; NSSO runs sample surveys in rounds. India runs on data!
teach.nudge: Good! You named one agency. Who runs the sample surveys on spending and jobs, and how often is the Census held?

revise.summary: India's main data agencies include the Census of India, NSSO, CSO, RGI, DGCIS and the Labour Bureau. The Census is the most complete source of demographic data; NSSO runs nationwide sample surveys in rounds.
focus: Match each type of data with its agency
Remember key Census years: every 10 years since 1881, first after independence in 1951
Know NSSO's surveys, its journal Sarvekshana and the 2019 merger into NSO
Know other sources like the Economic Survey and RBI publications
remember: Census: every 10 years since 1881; first after independence in 1951
NSSO (set up in 1950) publishes results in 'Sarvekshana'; in 2019 NSSO and CSO merged to form the NSO
CSO: national income; RGI: births and deaths; DGCIS: foreign trade; Labour Bureau: labour data
traps: Don't say the regular census began in 1951: that was the first after independence; regular census began in 1881
Don't think the Census runs the sample surveys in rounds: NSSO does
Don't link foreign trade data to the Census: DGCIS compiles them
